To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ThiS is a new UBL that can be covalently attached by an isopeptide bond to lysine residues on δ(32) in Escherichium coli.
δ(32), an essential transcription factor in Escherichiacoli, is degraded by proteases after being modified by a ubiquitin-like protein.
ThiS, a ubiquitin-like protein (UBL), is a novel substrate adaptor of the proteasome in Escherichiacoli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the discovery and characterization of the ThiS-δ(32) conjugation system in E. coli and the identification of other substrates of ThiS.
the discovery of a novel pathway for protein degradation in Escherichiacoli, which is mediated by an ubiquitin-like small protein modifier.
the ubiquitin-like protein modification of δ(32), which is the first report of this kind in bacteria, and provides new insights into protein quality control in bacteria.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ThiS is an ubiquitin-like modifier and that δ(32) is a substrate for degradation via the ThiS-protease system.
the ubiquitin-protein modifier ThiS is used to target the heat shock transcription factor δ(32) for proteolysis in Escherichiacoli.
ThiS, as an UBL, is involved in the degradation of δ(32) in E. coli.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

δ(32), a small protein, is a substrate of a ubiquitin-like protein modifier ThiS and is targeted for degradation in a similar way to the ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation pathway in eukaryotic cells.
δ(32) is modified by ThiS and then degraded by proteases, similar to the eukaryote UPS.
δ(32) is targeted for degradation by proteases through the covalent attachment of ThiS in a manner similar to the ubiquitin-dependent pathway in eukaryotic cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the degradation of proteins in E. coli, which has been thought to be ubiquitin independent, can be regulated by an ubiquitin-like modification.
prokaryotes can use small protein modifiers to target proteins for proteolysis.
the UPS in eukaryotic cells is likely to have evolved from the ThiS-proteasome pathway in prokaryotes.
